transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-06-03 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan McKay (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (BrightPath ML), Luca Rossi (BrightPath SRE), Ananya Patel (BrightPath Product)

Auto-summary: Quick review of last week's runs, new config proposals for continuous batching and concurrency, agreement on artifacts to share.

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, good to see you. quick agenda — 1) results from last week's baseline run, 2) priya's tuning proposals, 3) queueing sim/questions, and 4) next steps. should be 30ish minutes.

[00:25] Maya: yeah thanks. busy week but we got the baseline in — we saw average throughput of about 420 rps on the small 8-gpu pool, p95 around 320ms and p99 spiked to 1.1s on bursts.

[00:45] Priya: ok that matches what we saw, there was a lot of tail due to cold kv cache misses and some queuing behind the worker spin-up. i think we can shave a chunk by two levers: continuous batching and tuning concurrency thresholds.

[01:10] Luca: when you say continuous batching, are you referring to the micro-window approach or the auto-batch that's tied to token arrival? we tried something like that internally but had trouble with token-level jitter.

[01:30] Priya: yep micro-window — basically a short hold (like 5-50ms) to accumulate requests then flush. we can tune the window per model seq length distribution. aggressive window (50ms) improves throughput but raises median a bit, conservative (5ms) keeps latency tight.

[01:55] Maya: mm-hmm. our product is search so p95 matters more than absolute median, but p99 spikes are a problem for user experience. what's the expected p99 delta?

[02:12] Priya: from our internal sims, aggressive batching moved throughput +30-40% and p50 up ~20-40ms, p95 stable or slightly better, p99 can get worse if queue gets deep unless we cap concurrency and preempt long-running requests. there's a tradeoff.

[02:35] Jordan: right and remember Redwood's continuous batching also cooperates with KV caching — if prefix hits are warmed, effective per-token work drops and batching becomes more efficient.

[03:00] Ananya: can you remind us what warms the kv cache? like do we need a dedicated warm-up pass or is it on-demand?

[03:15] Priya: it's mostly on-demand but you can pre-warm by replaying representative prefixes — that's why we asked for a trace. warm cache reduces tail because fewer kv misses force longer compute. sometimes folks do a short warm-up job at pool start.

[03:40] Luca: we have questions on queueing — if we set concurrency too low we see request queuing at the gateway and client-side timeouts. how does redwood suggest handling gateway queues versus worker-side queues?

[04:00] Jordan: good point. our recommendation: boundary the gateway queue with backpressure and explicit queue-depth metrics; keep client retry/backoff sane. worker-side queueing is controlled by concurrency targets per GPU; if gateway queues are long it's often better to add a temporary burst capacity or nudge concurrency.

[04:25] Priya: also important — give us the request size distribution. batching efficiency depends a lot on seq length skew. a small set of long requests can dominate GPU time and blow up p99.

[04:45] Maya: sure, we'll upload anonymized 24h trace — contains sizes and timestamps. we'll scrub tokens.

[05:05] Jordan: perfect. so immediate plan — Redwood runs two configs: aggressive continuous batching (window 50ms) + concurrency cap tuned, and conservative (window 5ms) to compare. priya will capture p50/p95/p99 and throughput over 1h.

[05:25] Priya: i'll also instrument queue-depth, kv-cache hit rate, and worker utilization. expect CSV/timeseries in the spreadsheet.

[05:40] Luca: are you going to use the same model/quantization? we ran a 4-bit quantized variant last run.

[05:50] Priya: yes we keep model binary constant for apples-to-apples — same quantization, same kernel. only runtime batching and concurrency differ. any other env diffs?

[06:05] Maya: none from our side. curious about warmup strategies though — if we spin a dedicated pool will that help warm cache persistently?

[06:20] Jordan: Dedicated capacity keeps workers hot and you can keep the kv cache resident, which reduces misses. cost is higher but predictable. we can rough out cost delta after the throughput tests.

[06:40] Ananya: what's the ballpark delta for dedicated vs shared at our current throughput? even a rough number helps the business case.

[06:50] Jordan: i'll give a rough — but need to run throughput numbers first. we can do a back-of-envelope in about 48 hours after tests; then provide a dedicated pricing delta.

[07:10] Maya: ok. one more on telemetry — we need token-level breakdowns for cost attribution. is that available?

[07:25] Priya: token-level breakdown exists in the console but retention defaults are low. we can export the per-request cost/latency traces to CSV. we'll add that to the artifact set.

[07:40] Luca: regarding the queuing sim — if we provide a 24h trace, can you run a synthetic replay with gateway arrival patterns and show queue depth over time?

[07:55] Priya: yes we can run a replay sim and include a plot of queue-depth vs. concurrency. that'll demonstrate when p99 corners appear.

[08:10] Jordan: ok let's capture action items — jordan will post the shared spreadsheet link and initial run configs; priya will kick off the aggressive + conservative runs and attach telemetry; may/brightpath uploads trace; luca sends current concurrency limits and k8s spec.

[08:35] Maya: quick callout — we saw occasional misattributed speaker labels in the transcript previously so expect some noise in the autogenerated logs, but the metrics themselves are clean.

[08:50] Priya: noted. also a gotcha — if you have long tail requests that are compute-heavy, batching can actually make p99 worse because short requests wait behind a long one; we sometimes implement preemption or queue prioritization to avoid that.

[09:15] Ananya: preemption sounds complex — is that something you provide or we need engineering changes?

[09:30] Priya: Redwood runtime supports simple priority gating and soft preemption policies; for hard preemption you'd need a small change. we can propose a policy (e.g., cap single-request token limit or reserve slots for small requests).

[09:55] Jordan: to keep momentum, we'll do the two runs, share results, and schedule a deeper SRE-runbook session next week to discuss warmup and preemption. who should join from BrightPath?

[10:10] Luca: i'll be there and maya. maybe ananya for product context.

[10:25] Jordan: perfect. we'll aim for the week of 2025-06-09. I'll send invites.

[10:40] Maya: any other blockers? security/compliance was mentioned last time — we still need the SOC2 attestation but that's a separate thread.

[10:55] Jordan: yep i'll share the security pack in the CRM thread. not blocking the throughput tests.

[11:10] Priya: final note — when you upload the trace please include 95th-token-length percentile markers so we can tune windows per percentiles; that'll speed iteration.

[11:25] Maya: will do.

[11:35] Jordan: awesome, thanks everyone. recap in the sheet and i'll put next steps in calendar. see you next week.

End meeting.
